newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open weaker before jobless claims.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open weaker before jobless claims.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened slightly weaker on Thursday ahead of weekly data on new U.S. jobless claims.
Jobless claims figures are due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. They are expected to total 313,000 for the week ended April 5, little changed from 314,000 new claims a week earlier.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was down 3/32 to 94 even in early dealinings, yielding 7.11 percent.
Analysts said if jobless claims data come in as expected, they will reinforce concern about tight labor markets.

"If claims hold around where the markets are expecting, that leaves the very tight labor market condition in place and there will be reason to be concerned about what the Fed is thinking (in terms of further interest-rate tightenings)," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.
Stiles said volume was just moderate overnight.
"Certainly there has been steady talk of Japanese buying, but if they are buying, someone bigger is selling," he said.
Stiles said central bank and hedge fund selling emerges on upticks and that seems to be the bigger flow.
Longer term investors have taken a "very defensive" stance, Stiles said.

The market will have little to occupy its attention after the jobless claims numbers, Stiles said. No new data are due until Friday's reports on March wholesale prices (the Producer Price Index) and retail sales.
The PPI is expected to be unchanged and the core PPI, the index without its more volatile food and energy components, is
Retail sales for March are expected to be up 0.6 percent after a firm 0.8 percent gain in February.
Without auto sales, retail sales are expected to be up 0.4 percent after a 0.5 percent ex-autos gain in February.
Credit market participants will continue to watch the dollar, analysts said.

The dollar came off its peaks in early U.S. dealings, traading below 126 yen and 1.72 marks after Japan's Minister of Finance Mitsuzuka said the yen's recent fall was excessive and that Japan would deal decisively with excessive moves.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin is scheduled to be interviewed on CNBC television at 1030 EDT/1430 GMT.

Remarks by several Fed officials are also on tap for Thursday and the market will pay attention to the tone of their remarks. In Charleston, S.C., Richmond Federal Reserve President Alfred Broaddus will discuss the current economy at a luncheon sponsored by the Richmond Fed for its joint board at 1230 EDT/1630 GMT. In Dana Point, Calif., Chicago Federal Reserve President Michael Moskow delivers a speech on the future of people, technology and trade to the Association of Executive Search Consultants at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT.
Later, Fed Governor Susan Phillips will join a panel at Vanderbilt University to discuss the 1987 stock market crash.
At 1730 EDT/2130 GMT, Fed Governor Laurence Meyer will talk at a Bard College conference on financial structure.
In early dealings, three-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.09 percent. Six-month and year bill rates were each up one basis point to 5.36 percent and 5.64 percent, respectively.
Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 99-21/32, yielding 6.44 percent. Five-year notes were down 2/32 to 99-12/32, yielding 6.77 percent. Ten-year notes were off 3/32 to 95-10/32, yielding 6.91 percent.
